newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OLYMPICS-SWIMMING GREAT LENDS GENES FOR SYDNEY PINS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-SWIMMING GREAT LENDS GENES FOR SYDNEY PINS.

text.p: After giving blood, sweat and tears for her country, Australian swimming legend Dawn Fraser is now offering her DNA in support of the Sydney 2000 Olympics.
Sydney Games organisers said on Wednesday they had granted a licence to an Australian company that would offer collectors the chance to own a part of Fraser, albeit a microscopic one.

Aminco Australia, one of four official pin makers for the 2000 Games, plan to offer for sale a limited edition box of lapel pins impregnated with Fraser's DNA -- the molecules which form the body's chemical building blocks.
"DNA is used quite a lot in anti-counterfeiting techniques," Aminco chairman Kingsley Mundey told Reuters.

"Dawn Fraser is one of the greatest Olympians of all times and it became a logical progression (to use her DNA), because she is seen by most Australians as a symbol of an ordinary Australian achieving great things," he said.
Fraser's liquid DNA will be mixed into the pin in the production process, with 5,000 sets of five pins to go on sale for A$200 (US$156) next month.
Four of the pins in each box will contain the precious DNA, the molecules which fix a person's genetic make-up.
Mundey said he expected the value of the individual pins to increase dramatically by the time the Games begin on September 15, 2000.
"They should be worth a lot more because the DNA pins are a world-first," Mundey said.
Collecting souvenir pins has become an obsession at recent Games, with "pinheads" buying and swapping millions of dollars worth of Olympics-related pins from around the world.

Actress Demi Moore and U.S. President Bill Clinton's daughter Chelsea were numbered among the "pinheads" at last year's Atlanta Games, where an estimated 50 million pins were issued to commemorate the Games.
Fraser was the world's most successful swimmer for many years, winning the 100 metres Olympic freestyla in Melbourne in 1956, Rome in 1960 and Tokyo in 1964.
Hungary's Krisztina Egerszegi became the only other swimmer to win the same event at three consecutive Olympics when she won the 200 metres backstroke in Atlanta last year.
